title: Polynomial Rings, the Division Algorithm and Roots

items.title: The polynomial ring over a commutative ring as finitely supported coefficient sequences with convolution
items.strategy: For a commutative ring R, define R[x] as the set of functions a:N->R with finite support, write a as a formal sum, define addition coefficientwise and multiplication by finite convolution, and identify R with the constant polynomials while defining x as the sequence supported at 1.

items.title: Coefficientwise sums and convolution products of finitely supported sequences are finitely supported
items.strategy: Choose bounds beyond the supports of the two coefficient sequences. Addition vanishes beyond their maximum, while every summand in a convolution coefficient beyond the sum of the bounds contains a zero factor.

items.title: Polynomial convolution makes R[x] a commutative ring containing R as its constant subring
items.strategy: Verify the additive laws coefficientwise. For multiplication, use finite-sum reindexing to prove associativity, commutativity and distributivity, identify the sequence supported at 0 with value 1 as the identity, and verify that the constant-polynomial map is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

items.title: Degree, leading coefficient and monic polynomial, with the zero polynomial having no degree
items.strategy: For a nonzero finitely supported coefficient sequence, use the maximum of its nonempty support as the degree and its value there as the leading coefficient; call it monic when that value is 1. State explicitly that the zero polynomial has neither a degree nor a leading coefficient.

items.title: Finitely supported coefficient sequences and trimmed finite coefficient lists define the same formal polynomials
items.strategy: Send a nonzero finitely supported sequence to the unique list ending at its degree and send the zero sequence to the distinguished zero polynomial; pad a finite list by zeros in the reverse direction. Prove the maps are inverse and preserve addition, convolution, degree and leading coefficient.

items.title: Degree inequalities for sums and products over a commutative ring
items.strategy: For nonzero polynomials, inspect coefficients above the relevant support bounds. Prove deg(f+g)<=max(deg f,deg g) when f+g is nonzero, identify the coefficient of degree deg f+deg g in fg as the product of leading coefficients, and conclude deg(fg)<=deg f+deg g whenever fg is nonzero.

items.title: Over an integral domain, degrees add under multiplication of nonzero polynomials
items.strategy: The top convolution coefficient is the product of the two nonzero leading coefficients; the domain hypothesis makes it nonzero, while every higher coefficient vanishes by the support bounds.

items.title: A polynomial ring over an integral domain is an integral domain
items.strategy: Use the product-degree theorem to show that a product of two nonzero polynomials cannot vanish, and inherit commutativity and the distinct zero and identity through the constant-polynomial embedding.

items.title: The units of R[x] over an integral domain are exactly the constant polynomials whose values are units of R
items.strategy: If fg=1, degree additivity forces both factors to have degree 0; compare constant coefficients. Conversely, the constant polynomial attached to a unit has the constant inverse.

items.title: Evaluation and roots of a polynomial in a commutative target ring
items.strategy: Given a unital ring homomorphism phi:R->S between commutative rings and s in S, define f(s) as the finite sum of phi(a_i)s^i. A root is an s for which this value is 0; distinguish the formal polynomial from the element obtained by evaluation.

items.title: Universal property of R[x]: a coefficient homomorphism and the image of x determine a unique ring homomorphism
items.strategy: Show directly that evaluation preserves addition, identity and convolution multiplication, and verify that the formula agrees with evaluation of the corresponding trimmed coefficient list. Any homomorphism extending phi and sending x to s must send each finite sum of monomials to the evaluation formula, proving uniqueness.

items.title: Polynomial rings in finitely many commuting indeterminates by iteration
items.strategy: Define R[x_1,...,x_n] recursively by R[x_1,...,x_0]=R and adjoining one polynomial indeterminate at a time. Record the canonical coefficient inclusions and that the iteration makes all named indeterminates commute.

items.title: A polynomial ring in finitely many indeterminates over an integral domain is an integral domain
items.strategy: Induct on the number of indeterminates, using the one-variable domain-inheritance result at the successor step and treating the zero-variable ring as R.

items.title: Division by a monic polynomial over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Induct on the degree of the dividend. If its degree is below the monic divisor, stop; otherwise subtract the leading coefficient times the appropriate power of x times the divisor to lower the degree. Prove existence and uniqueness over every commutative coefficient ring; for uniqueness, monicity keeps the top coefficient of the divisor times a nonzero quotient difference nonzero even when the ring has zero divisors.

items.title: Factor theorem over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Divide f by the monic polynomial x-a. The remainder is constant, and evaluating the division identity at a identifies that constant with f(a), giving f(a)=0 iff x-a divides f.

items.title: Division algorithm for polynomials over a field
items.strategy: Normalize a nonzero divisor g by its invertible leading coefficient to a monic polynomial, apply monic division, and absorb the scalar into the quotient. Degree additivity over the field proves uniqueness, including zero dividend and constant divisor cases.

items.title: For every field F, F[x] is a Euclidean domain with degree as Euclidean function
items.strategy: Combine the domain theorem with the division algorithm and take the degree of each nonzero polynomial as its natural-valued Euclidean function; the remainder is zero or has smaller degree.

items.title: For every field F, F[x] is a principal ideal domain
items.strategy: Apply the published theorem that every Euclidean domain is a PID to the preceding Euclidean structure.

items.title: The monic greatest common divisor of two polynomials over a field
items.strategy: For f and g not both zero, define gcd(f,g) as the unique monic generator of the principal ideal (f,g). Relate this ideal definition to the divisibility characterization and explicitly leave gcd(0,0) undefined.

items.title: Bézout identity and the Euclidean algorithm for polynomials over a field
items.strategy: Run repeated division until the last nonzero remainder, back-substitute to express it as Af+Bg, and normalize it to be monic. Prove that it divides f and g and that every common divisor divides it, agreeing with the ideal-defined gcd.

items.title: Every irreducible polynomial over a field is prime
items.strategy: If irreducible p divides fg and does not divide f, then gcd(p,f)=1. Bézout gives Ap+Bf=1; multiply by g and use p|fg to obtain p|g.

items.title: Every nonzero nonunit polynomial over a field factors into irreducible polynomials
items.strategy: Use strong induction on degree. An irreducible polynomial is the base alternative; a reducible polynomial is a product of two nonunits of strictly smaller positive degree, to which the induction hypothesis applies.

items.title: For every field F, F[x] is a unique factorisation domain
items.strategy: Existence is the preceding induction lemma. For uniqueness, use that every irreducible is prime to divide one factor on the other side, cancel associates in the domain, and induct on the number of irreducible factors, including units and constants.

items.title: For a nonconstant p in F[x], the ideal (p) is maximal and F[x]/(p) is a field exactly when p is irreducible
items.strategy: If p is irreducible, every polynomial not divisible by p has gcd 1 with p, so Bézout gives an inverse for its residue class. Conversely, a nontrivial factorization produces nonzero nonunits or zero divisors in the quotient. Reconcile the conclusion with the published maximal-ideal/field-quotient equivalence.

items.title: A nonzero polynomial of degree n over an integral domain has at most n distinct roots
items.strategy: Induct on degree. If there is a root a, factor f=(x-a)q; every other root b satisfies (b-a)q(b)=0, and the domain plus b!=a forces q(b)=0. The zero-degree case has no roots.

items.title: Over an infinite integral domain, equal polynomial functions come from equal polynomials
items.strategy: If f and g agree at every element, then f-g has infinitely many roots. The root bound forces f-g to be the zero polynomial.

items.title: A polynomial of degree two or three over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in the field
items.strategy: A root gives a linear factor by the factor theorem. Conversely, a nontrivial factorization of total degree two or three has a degree-one factor; normalize it to x-a and recover a root.

items.title: The formal derivative of a polynomial
items.strategy: For f=sum a_i x^i, define f' by giving the coefficient of x^(i-1) as the ring multiple i a_i for positive i. State the constant and zero cases and use numerals as ring multiples, never an applied canonical-embedding notation.

items.title: Linearity, power rule, Leibniz rule and the degree bound for the formal derivative
items.strategy: Compare coefficients to prove additivity and the monomial power rule. For the product rule, reindex the convolution and split the coefficient multiplier i+j into its two additive parts. Inspect the support formula to prove that a nonzero derivative has degree strictly below that of the original nonconstant polynomial.

items.title: Repeated roots in extension fields and separable polynomials
items.strategy: For a field F contained as a subfield of E and nonzero f in F[x], call a in E a repeated root when (x-a)^2 divides f in E[x]. Call f separable over F when it has no repeated root in any extension field, and record the constant-polynomial convention.

items.title: A root is repeated exactly when it is also a root of the formal derivative
items.strategy: Differentiate f=(x-a)q to get f'=q+(x-a)q'. If f is divisible by (x-a)^2, both evaluations vanish. Conversely, f(a)=f'(a)=0 first gives f=(x-a)q and then q(a)=0, so the factor theorem gives a second factor x-a.

items.title: The monic gcd of two base-field polynomials is unchanged after extending the coefficient field
items.strategy: Factor out the base-field gcd and use its Bézout identity to show the remaining factors stay coprime over the extension. Hence no new positive-degree common factor appears; monic normalization fixes the associate.

items.title: A nonzero polynomial over a field is separable exactly when its gcd with its derivative is 1
items.strategy: If a repeated root occurs in an extension, the derivative criterion and gcd stability show the base gcd is nontrivial. Conversely, if the gcd has an irreducible factor p, pass to the field F[x]/(p), first checking that the constant-polynomial map embeds F because p is nonconstant; the residue class of x is then a common root of f and f', hence a repeated root.

items.title: An irreducible polynomial over a field is separable exactly when its derivative is nonzero
items.strategy: For irreducible f, any monic gcd of f and f' is 1 or the monic associate of f. Since deg f'<deg f whenever f' is nonzero, the second case occurs exactly when f'=0; apply the separability criterion.

items.title: Content and primitive integer polynomials
items.strategy: Use the unique trimmed coefficient list and define its finite gcd recursively from the published binary integer gcd, starting with 0; for a nonzero integer polynomial this gives a positive content. Call the polynomial primitive when its content is 1, separate the sign into a unit, and state the convention for nonzero constant polynomials.

items.title: Content is the positive common divisor of the coefficients divisible by every common divisor
items.strategy: Induct along the trimmed coefficient list using the published binary-gcd characterization. Prove that the recursive gcd divides every coefficient and that every common divisor of all coefficients divides it; for a nonzero polynomial it is positive. If the polynomial is not primitive, apply integer unique factorisation to obtain a prime divisor of its content and hence of every coefficient.

items.title: The product of primitive integer polynomials is primitive, and contents multiply
items.strategy: If a prime divided every coefficient of a product of two primitive polynomials, reduce modulo that prime and use that the polynomial ring over the resulting field is a domain. Then factor out the positive contents and compare signs to obtain c(fg)=c(f)c(g).

items.title: Gauss lemma: primitive factorisations over Q can be cleared to primitive factorisations over Z
items.strategy: Clear denominators from a rational factorization, extract positive contents from the resulting integer factors, and use content multiplicativity plus primitivity of f to cancel the scalar. Conclude that a primitive integer polynomial is irreducible over Q exactly when it is irreducible over Z.

items.title: Rational root theorem
items.strategy: Write a rational root in lowest terms as p/q with q positive. Multiply f(p/q)=0 by q^n; the coprime-divides-product lemma shows p divides the constant coefficient and q divides the leading coefficient. Include constant-zero and monic specializations without applying a canonical embedding to an index.

items.title: Irreducibility after reduction modulo a prime implies irreducibility over Q when the leading coefficient survives
items.strategy: For a primitive integer polynomial whose leading coefficient is not divisible by prime p, any rational factorization clears by Gauss to an integer factorization. Reduction modulo p preserves the degrees of both factors and contradicts irreducibility of the reduced polynomial.

items.title: Eisenstein criterion over the integers
items.strategy: Assume a primitive integer polynomial has leading coefficient not divisible by p, all lower coefficients divisible by p, and constant coefficient not divisible by p^2. Clear a hypothetical rational factorization by Gauss, reduce modulo p to force both positive-degree factors to have constant terms divisible by p, and contradict the constant coefficient condition.

items.title: For every prime p and positive n, x^n-p is irreducible over Q
items.strategy: Apply Eisenstein at p: the leading coefficient is 1, every lower nonconstant coefficient is 0, and the constant coefficient -p is divisible by p but not p^2. Check n=1 explicitly.

items.title: Formal polynomials are not the functions they induce
items.strategy: Explain that equality in R[x] is coefficientwise, while evaluation produces a function only after choosing a target ring. Over an infinite domain evaluation is injective by the root bound, but over finite rings distinct polynomials can induce the same function, as the companion counterexample shows.

title: Polynomial Rings and Roots: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Polynomial addition and multiplication computed from coefficient convolution
items.strategy: Represent two explicit low-degree polynomials by coefficient sequences, compute their coordinatewise sum and each convolution coefficient, and verify the familiar expanded product without treating x as a variable value.

items.title: Long division, the Euclidean algorithm and a Bézout identity in Q[x]
items.strategy: Choose an explicit pair of rational polynomials, carry out successive divisions to the last nonzero remainder, normalize the gcd to monic, and back-substitute to display concrete Bézout coefficients.

items.title: Over Z/4, a nonconstant polynomial can be a unit and product degree can drop
items.strategy: In (Z/4)[x], compute (1+2x)^2=1. Thus 1+2x is its own inverse even though it is nonconstant, and two degree-one factors have a degree-zero product because the top coefficient 4 vanishes.

items.title: Division with a degree-small remainder can fail over Z when the divisor's leading coefficient is not a unit
items.strategy: Try to divide the constant polynomial 1 by the constant nonunit 2 in Z[x]. A remainder of degree below 0 must be zero, which would require 1=2q for an integer polynomial q, an impossibility.

items.title: Quadratics can have four roots over Z/6 and Z/8
items.strategy: Over Z/6, check that x^2-x vanishes at 0, 1, 3 and 4; over Z/8, check that x^2-1 vanishes at 1, 3, 5 and 7. These witnesses isolate the missing domain hypothesis in the root bound while the factor theorem remains valid.

items.title: Over F_p, x^p-x and the zero polynomial induce the same function but are distinct polynomials
items.strategy: Use Fermat's little theorem to show a^p-a=0 for every residue class a modulo prime p, while the coefficient of x^p proves that x^p-x is not the zero polynomial. Include p=2 and the positive-degree boundary explicitly.

items.title: The polynomial x^2-2 is irreducible over Q
items.strategy: First check from the integer divisor bound and discreteness that 2 is prime, hence its integer divisors are exactly plus or minus 1 and plus or minus 2. The rational-root theorem restricts a rational root to those four candidates; direct evaluation excludes them, and the quadratic criterion gives irreducibility.

items.title: The polynomial x^2+1 is irreducible over R
items.strategy: The ordered-field laws give a^2>=0 for every real a, so a^2+1 is positive and never zero. Apply the quadratic criterion, without making any assertion here about factorisation over the complex numbers.

items.title: Reduction modulo 2 proves x^3+17x+391 irreducible over Q
items.strategy: First check from the integer divisor bound and discreteness that 2 is prime. Reduce to x^3+x+1 over F_2, check its two possible values are nonzero, use the cubic criterion for irreducibility over F_2, and apply the reduction theorem.

items.title: Eisenstein proves x^n-2 irreducible over Q for every positive n
items.strategy: First check from the integer divisor bound and discreteness that 2 is prime. Then verify the Eisenstein hypotheses at 2 uniformly for positive n, including n=1, and apply the criterion.

items.title: Translation turns x^4+1 into an Eisenstein polynomial
items.strategy: Use the polynomial universal property to show substitution x->x+1 is an automorphism with inverse x->x-1. Expand (x+1)^4+1 and apply Eisenstein at 2, then transport irreducibility back to x^4+1.

items.title: A degree-four polynomial can be reducible over Q without having a rational root
items.strategy: Factor x^4+3x^2+2=(x^2+1)(x^2+2) in Q[x]. Since a rational square is nonnegative, neither quadratic factor has a rational root, so the product has none despite being reducible.

items.title: In characteristic 2, x^2+1=(x+1)^2 has zero derivative and a repeated root
items.strategy: Work in (Z/2)[x], compute the square and the formal derivative coefficientwise, and check the derivative criterion at the root 1.

items.title: For a field F, the ideal (x,y) in F[x,y] is not principal
items.strategy: If (x,y)=(d), then d divides both x and y. Compare degrees in each indeterminate to show every common divisor is a unit; that would make the ideal the whole ring, contradicted by evaluation at x=y=0.
